newsitem.title: UK: Malaria disaster looms over Africa, experts warn.
newsitem.headline: Malaria disaster looms over Africa, experts warn.

text.p: A malaria catastrophe is threatening Africa and the disease could spread uncontrollably if industrialised and developing nations do not start coordinating research, experts warned on Wednesday.

More than a dozen representatives of groups ranging from the World Health Organisation (WHO) to the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) signed a letter published in Nature magazine calling for more collaboration on developing drugs and vaccines.

"The international community has a responsibility to recognise malaria, like the AIDS pandemic, as a major challenge and commit itself to do more to prevent the disaster that looms over Africa," the letter said.

Those signing the letter included Richard Feachem of the World Bank, Harold Varmus, director of the U.S. Institute of Health, Maxime Schwartz, director of France's Institute Pasteur, George Radda, chief executive of Britain's Medical Research Council, Robert Mshana of the OAU and Tore Godal of the WHO.
"Malaria has been a problem for too long," they wrote. "More than a million people still die from it every year, most of them young children. Nine out of 10 of these deaths occur in Africa."

Resistance to malaria drugs like chloroquine was spreading, making the need for new drugs and vaccines urgent, they said. "New approaches are needed to control malaria and its mosquito vectors," they added. "One unprecedented opportunity to boost research in Africa at a relatively modest cost is offered by the Internet." Research centres in Africa should get access to e-mail right away, they said.
The coming months offered a good chance to plan better coordination for fighting malaria.

The OAU would put malaria on its agenda at its annual summit for the first time this year and the G7 group of industrialised nations (Britain, Japan, Canada, France, Germany, Italy and the United States) would also discuss malaria and other diseases this year.

In a special feature, Nature pointed out that malaria kills one person every 12 seconds and infects up to 500 million. Malaria was coming back in countries that had beat back the threat, and the mosquito that carries the responsible parasite was becoming resistant to pesticides.
WHO, the World Bank, the U.S. Centres for Disease Control and other agencies were discussing a 30-year, inter-organisational effort to battle malaria, Nature said.
So far vaccines have been disappointing but Nature said one being developed by SmithKline Beecham Biologicals and the U.S. Army's Walter Reed Hospital was offering hope.
